children: Iron ore futures traded in a narrow range on Tuesday, as support from rising freight costs countered pressure from a weak near-term demand outlook.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
traded 0.14% higher at 716.5 yuan ($107.01) a metric ton, as of 0220 GMT.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.15% higher at $97.15 a ton.

Mainstream route freight rates rose across the board as of September 21, with the Capesize C5 route from Australia up $0.1 a ton and the C3 route from Brazil up $0.2 a ton, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.

Rising freight costs feed into ore prices through landed costs, particularly for longer-haul cargoes such as Brazilian and non-mainstream ore, analysts from broker Huatai Futures said, adding that this is helping support a floor under prices.
Oil prices, a key part of shipping costs, gained after several days of declines, as markets watched possible US-Iran talks at the United Nations General Assembly this week.

End-use demand has yet to reach a turning point, and iron ore demand is unlikely to improve in the near term and prices are likely to stay rangebound with a weaker bias, analysts from Shanghai Metals Market said in a note.

China's domestic steel demand will fluctuate downwards over the next decade, though it will likely remain above 800 million tons during the 15th Five-Year Plan before falling below that level by 2035, Liu Jian, president of the China Iron and Steel Association, said on Sunday.
Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE rose, with coking coal
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were stronger. Rebar
